reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A malformation of late cortical organisation in which the cortex forms excessive small, fused gyri with abnormal lamination, producing an irregular or bumpy cortical surface
It is often bilateral and symmetric in recognised patterns, the perisylvian region being the most common site, giving the bilateral perisylvian syndrome
MRI shows an irregular grey-white junction with numerous small gyri; the cortex may look deceptively thickened because the tiny folds are packed together

Causes are heterogeneous and include genetic variants such as GPR56 and tubulin genes, chromosomal disorders including 22q11.2 deletion, and acquired insults, notably congenital cytomegalovirus infection and in-utero ischaemia
The bilateral perisylvian form typically causes pseudobulbar palsy with oromotor dysfunction, dysarthria, feeding difficulty, epilepsy, and variable cognitive impairment
Clinical severity depends on extent and location, ranging from focal, minimally symptomatic lesions to widespread malformation with severe disability
Diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern combined with genetic testing and evaluation for congenital infection
reference.pathophysiology: Polymicrogyria is a disorder of the late stages of cortical development, arising after neurons have largely completed migration, during cortical organisation and lamination. Both genetic factors, including variants in genes governing the neuronal cytoskeleton and cortical patterning, and acquired prenatal insults such as congenital cytomegalovirus infection or focal ischaemia can disrupt normal gyral formation. The cortex develops an excess of small, abnormally laminated and fused convolutions. The distribution of the malformation, often bilateral and region-specific, determines the neurological consequences such as perisylvian oromotor dysfunction and epilepsy.
additionalDifferentials: Schizencephaly, which is frequently lined by polymicrogyria
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution brain MRI to define the distribution and extent of the malformation
Testing for congenital cytomegalovirus infection, including stored newborn blood spot analysis where available
Chromosomal microarray, including assessment for 22q11.2 deletion
Gene panel or exome sequencing for cortical malformation genes
Swallowing and speech assessment for perisylvian involvement
redFlags: Severe oromotor dysfunction with aspiration and feeding failure
Evidence of congenital cytomegalovirus infection with hearing loss requiring intervention
Rapidly progressive neurological decline suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome ranges widely with the extent and location of involvement. Small focal lesions may be asymptomatic or cause only focal epilepsy, whereas extensive bilateral malformation causes significant motor, oromotor, cognitive, and seizure disability.
pitfalls: Misreading the packed small gyri as a thick, smooth cortex and mistaking it for pachygyria
Failing to test for congenital cytomegalovirus, an important and potentially preventable acquired cause
Overlooking associated 22q11.2 deletion and its systemic implications
Assuming all polymicrogyria is genetic and neglecting acquired prenatal causes in counselling
